Good morning, Ryan. Thank you for coming to this job interview. Can you hear me well?
Good morning! Yes, perfectly. Thank you for the invitation.
So, what do you do in your current job?
I’m an HR assistant at a retail company. I help with payroll and I organize the training calendar.
How much experience do you have in HR, and why did you choose this area?
Four years. I studied psychology, and I always liked to work with people.
What is your biggest strength? And one weakness?
My strength is organization. My weakness... I sometimes say yes to too many projects.
Thank you, Ryan. You are on our shortlist. We will follow up by Friday.

Hi, I'm Oliver, and I'm an HR director in London. I do about twenty job interviews every month, and I always ask the same three questions. First: what do you do in your current job? I want to hear the person describe a normal day. Second: tell me about a difficult moment at work. What happened, and what did you do? I ask this because I want to know how the person solves problems. And my last question is always: what questions do you have for me? A good candidate always has questions. When somebody says no questions, I am a little worried.

Hello, I'm Ingrid, and I'm from Gothenburg, in Sweden. Last year I had a job interview for a training manager position. The interviewer was very kind. She asked: what do you do in your current job? That was easy. Then she asked: why did you leave your last company? I was not ready for that question, and I talked for five minutes about my old boss. It was a mistake. The next day I sent an email to follow up and to thank her. I was on the shortlist, but I didn't get the job. Now I always prepare a short, positive answer for that question.
